title: Elementary Matrices
description: Recognizing elementary matrices, identifying the row operation each one encodes, and finding the inverse of an elementary matrix (Anton 1.5).

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 3\times3 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: It is elementary: it's the identity matrix after Add $-3\,R_{3}$ to $R_{1}$ -- exactly one row operation.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 2\times2 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: It is elementary: it's the identity matrix after Add $-2\,R_{2}$ to $R_{1}$ -- exactly one row operation.

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: It is elementary: it's the identity matrix after Subtract $R_{2}$ from $R_{1}$ -- exactly one row operation.

explanations: It is elementary: it's the identity matrix after Multiply $R_{1}$ by $4$ -- exactly one row operation.

explanations: It is elementary: it's the identity matrix after Multiply $R_{2}$ by $-3$ -- exactly one row operation.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 2\times2 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- two different rows are each scaled -- that's two row operations combined, not one.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 3\times3 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- one row has more than one nonzero off-diagonal entry -- that combines a scale and an addition, not a single operation.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 2\times2 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- it has a zero row, so it isn't even invertible -- an elementary matrix is always invertible.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 3\times3 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- it has two identical rows, so it's singular -- an elementary matrix is always invertible.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a 2\times2 elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- it has a zero row, so it isn't even invertible -- an elementary matrix is always invertible.

questions.prompt:
Is the following a $3\times3$ elementary matrix?

$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
explanations: Not quite -- this permutation matrix cycles all three rows. It's a product of *two* row swaps, not a single elementary row operation.

questions.prompt:
This 3\times3 matrix is the identity matrix after ONE elementary row operation. Which row operation was applied?

$\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
questions.explanation: Compare column by column to the identity matrix: the only change is consistent with 'Multiply $R_{1}$ by $-1$'.

questions.prompt:
This 2\times2 elementary matrix corresponds to: Add $2\,R_{1}$ to $R_{2}$.

What is its inverse?

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
questions.explanation: An elementary matrix's inverse just undoes the row operation. Since this one is 'Add $2\,R_{1}$ to $R_{2}$', the inverse is the matrix for the operation that reverses it.
